MRI showed a pituitary adenoma with suprasellar extension (see Fig. 1.5).

{{image}}

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate definitive management approach for him?**
explanation_md: In view of a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm and leading to visual-field defects, the patient needs to be referred to neurosurgeons for elective trans-sphenoidal surgery. His biochemical results are consistent with secondary hypogonadism and hypothyroidism. In a compressive pituitary adenoma, somatotrophs and gonadotrophs are the first cell lines to be affected, with thyrotroph and corticotroph involvement at later stages.

stem_md:
A 22-year-old woman presented with a history of menstrual irregularities for the previous 4 years. She had attained menarche at the age of 13 years. Her general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable. Ultrasound of the pelvis showed bilateral enlarged and cystic ovaries. MRI of the pituitary showed an 18-mm pituitary tumour without any involvement of the optic chiasm.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| FSH | 45 U/L | (follicular 0.5–5, mid-cycle 8–33, luteal 2–8) |
| LH | 2.5 U/L | (follicular 3–12, mid-cycle 20–80, luteal 3–16) |
| Oestradiol | 1332 pmol/L | (follicular 17–260, luteal 180–1100) |
| Prolactin | 604 mU/L | (45–375) |

**Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis in her case?**

options.E: Polycystic ovarian syndrome with a pituitary incidentaloma

explanation_md: This patient has an elevated oestradiol level in the presence of high FSH and low LH levels, together with the presence of pituitary macroadenoma on MRI of the pituitary, suggestive of diagnosis of a gonadotropin (FSH) secretory adenoma. It is an extremely rare tumour, and can present with enlarged ovaries and menstrual irregularities, and may initially be erroneously labelled as polycystic ovarian syndrome. The oestrogen levels may be high or within normal range. LH levels are usually suppressed. The treatment remains elective surgery to remove the pituitary adenoma.

stem_md:
A 47-year-old post-menopausal woman presented to the endocrine clinic with a 6-month history of palpitations, increasing shortness of breath, and weight loss. Her general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable. Her thyroid function test (TFT) results were as shown:

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| FT4 | 24.8 pmol/L | (9.0–19.1) |
| FT3 | 7.4 pmol/L | (2.6–5.7) |
| TSH | 6.15 mU/L | (0.35–5.0) |

**Which one of the following clinical/biochemical features is consistent with a diagnosis of TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (TSHoma)?**

options.D: Non-suppression of TSH on T3 suppression test

explanation_md: TSH-secreting tumours are rare causes of thyrotoxicosis and comprise 0.7–9% of all pituitary adenoma. These tumours need to be distinguished from thyroid hormone resistance syndromes, which present with similar TFT results (elevated or inappropriately normal TSH levels, in the presence of raised FT4 and FT3). Clinically, these patients might have features of mild hyperthyroidism with goitre present in the majority of the patients. The SHBG levels are usually elevated. TSHomas are characterized by a raised α subunit/TSH ratio >1, usually a macroadenoma on MRI of the pituitary, and a lack of elevation of TSH after a TRH stimulation test. T3 fails to suppress TSH in patients with TSHoma.

stem_md:
A 66-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of weight loss, increased sweating, and palpitations. His general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable except for mild resting tremors and the presence of a small goitre. His TFT results were as shown:

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| FT3 | 6.5 pmol/L | (2.6–5.7) |
| FT4 | 25.0 pmol/L | (11.5–22.7) |
| TSH | 5.8 mU/L | (0.35–5.5) |

**Which one of the following will be a useful test to establish the possible underlying diagnosis?**
explanation_md:
In patients presenting with suspected TSHoma or thyroid hormone resistance (as suggested by elevated FT4/FT3 and inappropriately high/normal TSH), the first step is to exclude the presence of heterophile antibodies and non-thyroidal illness and get the TFT repeated in 4–6 weeks.

| Investigation | TSHoma | RTH |
|---|---|---|
| α subunit/TSH ratio | >1 | Not increased |
| Anterior pituitary hormones | May be abnormal | Normal |
| TRH test | Blunted TSH response | TSH increased |
| T3 suppression test | No TSH suppression | TSH suppressed partially |
| Somatostatin test | FT4 ↓ >30% | No FT4 decrease |

stem_md:
A 78-year-old man was referred to the endocrine clinic with a 6-month history of weight loss, increased sweating, and tremors. He had a background history of severe congestive cardiac failure and end-stage renal failure. On examination, he had a smooth small goitre, bilateral tremors, and bi-basal crepitations on auscultation of the lungs.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| FT4 | 26.5 pmol/L | (11.5–22.7 pmol/L) |
| FT3 | 9.1 pmol/L | (3.5–6.5 pmol/L) |
| TSH | 8.5 mU/L | (0.35–5.5 mU/L) |

The remaining anterior pituitary hormone profile was within normal range. Heterophile antibodies were negative. MRI of the pituitary showed a 15-mm pituitary adenoma, which was not compressing the optic chiasm. During the combined neurosurgical-endocrine multidisciplinary team meeting, a decision was made to manage him with medical therapy, considering his co-morbidities.

**Which one of the following is the treatment of choice for his further management?**
explanation_md: TSHoma are rare pituitary tumours with a prevalence of about one case per million. Most of these patients receive anti-thyroid treatment, initially due to an erroneous diagnosis of hyperthyroidism. TSHomas, due to their insidious onset and delay in diagnosis, are generally macroadenomas. Surgical treatment remains the treatment of choice. Octreotide therapy is the medical treatment in patients who are unresponsive to surgical therapy or who are deemed unfit for an operation.

stem_md:
Non-functioning pituitary adenoma (NFPA) are the commonest pituitary tumours, which account for approximately 90% of sellar masses, and may be detected incidentally or present with pressure symptoms.

**Which one of the following is the commonest pattern/finding seen on immunostaining of a NFPA?**
explanation_md: Gonadotropins are the commonest cells of origin for NPFA on immunocytochemical staining. Most of these tumours synthesize and secrete glycoprotein hormones and/or free α or β subunits. In a NFPA, the gonadotropin subunits are either secreted in low levels to have any clinical/functional significance or are biologically inert at gonadal level.

stem_md:
A 36-year-old woman was incidentally detected to have a 6-mm pituitary micro-adenoma on MRI of the head arranged to evaluate the cause for her recurrent headaches. Apart from the headaches that she had suffered for the previous 6 months, she had no past history of any significant medical illness and was not on any regular medications. Her general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable.

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?**
explanation_md:
With the advent of radiological imaging techniques, the incidence and prevalence of pituitary incidentaloma (PI) is increasing. The prevalence of micro-incidentaloma (size <10 mm) and macro-incidentaloma (size >10 mm) has been quoted between 5–30% and 0.1–0.25%, respectively, based on the modality used for scanning.

According to the guidelines (2011) from the Endocrine Society, patients with PI should undergo a complete history-taking and physical examination to evaluate for hormone over-/under-secretion, together with laboratory evaluation of anterior pituitary hormone function test. This is based on the fact that there is a high prevalence of subclinical disease, even in asymptomatic patients. A formal visual-field assessment is recommended only in patients with visual-field defects or a tumour compressing the optic nerve or chiasm on initial radiology.

stem_md:
A 41-year-old man was incidentally detected to have a pituitary tumour measuring 5 mm on a CT scan of the head done after a traumatic head injury. He had no significant past medical history and was not on any regular medications. His general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| IGF-1 | 30 nmol/L | (16–118) |
| Prolactin | 262 mU/L | (60–620) |
| Testosterone | 9.4 nmol/L | (8.5–28.5) |
| FT4 | 15.5 pmol/L | (11.5–22.7) |
| TSH | 3.0 mU/L | (0.35–5.5) |
| 9 a.m. cortisol | 423 nmol/L | - |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate step with regard to his further management considering he remains asymptomatic?**

options.B: Repeat MRI of the pituitary after 4 months
options.C: Repeat MRI of the pituitary after 1 year
options.D: Repeat MRI of the pituitary/anterior pituitary hormone profile after 4 months
options.E: Repeat MRI of the pituitary/anterior pituitary hormone profile after 1 year

explanation_md:
According to the Endocrine Society guidelines (2011), in patients with a pituitary micro-incidentaloma, MRI of the pituitary gland should be repeated after 1 year (after 6 months in patients with a macro-incidentaloma). If the repeat scan does not show any interval change in the size of the tumour, then subsequent scans should be organized every 1–2 years for the first 3 years and less frequently thereafter. In patients with macro-incidentaloma, yearly scans should be arranged for the first 3 years after initial diagnosis.

In a patient with micro-incidentaloma, a repeat anterior pituitary hormone profile is not routinely indicated. An anterior pituitary hormone profile should be repeated in patients displaying features of hormone deficiency/excess based on history and examination, or if there is an increase in size of the tumour on repeat radiological investigations.

stem_md:
A 35-year-old woman was reviewed at the endocrine clinic on a follow-up visit. She had been incidentally diagnosed as having a pituitary incidentaloma measuring 5 mm following investigations for a possible benign intracranial hypertension about 6 months before. She complained of recurrent episodes of headache together with visual disturbance during this visit. On examination, she had bitemporal superior quadrantanopia. Repeat MRI showed significant increase in the size of pituitary tumour, with compression of the optic chiasm.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| IGF-1 | 12 nmol/L | (16–118) |
| Prolactin | 950 mU/L | (60–620) |
| FT4 | 10.6 pmol/L | (11.5–22.7) |
| TSH | 0.5 mU/L | (0.35–5.5) |
| 9 a.m. cortisol | 401 nmol/L | - |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?**
explanation_md:
The indications for surgery in patients with PI include:

- The presence of a visual-field defect
- A lesion compressing the optic nerve or chiasm
- Ophthalmoplegia secondary to PI
- Pituitary apoplexy with severe visual disturbance
- Functional tumours (ACTH, GH-secreting)

stem_md:
A 16-year-old was reviewed in a joint paediatric to adult endocrine transition clinic. He was diagnosed as having craniopharyngioma at age 14 years and underwent surgical removal of the tumour. Post-operatively, he was noticed to have delayed growth (as evidenced by his height being two standard deviations (SDs) below normal, compared with other children his age). Both his parents were of average height and none of his siblings were of short stature. On an insulin tolerance test, a peak GH value of 3 mU/L (1 µg/L) was seen.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| 0-hour cortisol | 308 nmol/L | - |
| 30 minutes post-ACTH | 592 nmol/L | - |
| IGF-1 | 12 nmol/L | (16–118) |
| Prolactin | 145 mU/L | (45–375) |
| Testosterone | 11.2 nmol/L | (8.5–28.5) |
| TSH | 2.6 mU/L | (0.35–5.5) |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate approach for potential GH therapy in his case?**

options.A: Confirm the GH deficiency by a second dynamic test
options.B: GH replacement is contraindicated considering the history of craniopharyngioma
options.C: GH replacement is not required as the dynamic test results are normal
options.E: Start on GH replacement only if he is symptomatic

explanation_md: This boy has GH deficiency as a post-operative complication of craniopharyngioma resection as evidenced by delayed growth, low IGF-1 levels, and peak GH <6.7 ug/L. GH injections are given subcutaneously, with the dose in children generally being 0.7–1 mg/m2/day. The dose titration is based on IGF-1 levels. The main side effects associated with GH injections include fluid retention, myalgia, arthralgia, and benign intracranial hypertension. It is contraindicated in the presence of any active malignancy in the body. The GH therapy has been observed to be safe in children and young adults with craniopharyngioma.

stem_md:
A 20-year-old woman was referred to the endocrine clinic with a history of persistent headache over the previous year. Her examination showed evidence of a left temporal visual-field defect. Subsequent anterior pituitary functions confirmed secondary hypothyroidism and hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. MRI of the pituitary showed a 4 × 2 cm cystic parasellar lesion, which was compressing the optic chiasm. CT scan of the head showed calcification in the sellar region.

**Which one of the following is the likely diagnosis based on her clinical profile?**
explanation_md:
Craniopharyngiomas are characterized by the presence of an enhancing suprasellar mass, which may be cystic, and show calcification on a CT scan. These tumours may lead to the development of hormonal deficiencies (especially cranial DI due to ADH deficiency), growth retardation in children/young adults, or may present with local pressure effects. The cysts within the tumour are filled with protein and/or cholesterol, which are usually demonstrated as a T1 high-intensity signal on MRI. Management involves neurosurgery and radiotherapy.

| Characteristics | Adamantinomatous | Papillary |
|---|---|---|
| Age distribution | Bimodal (5–15 yrs & 45–60 yrs) | 5th–6th decade |
| Somatic mutation | CTNNB1 encoding β catenin | BRAF V600E |
| Recurrence rate | Higher | Relatively lower |

stem_md:
A 23-year-old woman presented to the endocrine clinic with a 6-week history of headaches, extreme fatigue, and malaise. She was in the post-partum period, having delivered 3 months before. Her general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable. MRI of the pituitary showed an enhancing mass with thickening of the pituitary stalk and loss of posterior pituitary bright spot.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| 0-hour cortisol | 55 nmol/L | - |
| 30-minute cortisol (post-synthetic ACTH injection) | 135 nmol/L | - |
| Prolactin | 801 mU/L | (100–550) |
| FT4 | 9.2 pmol/L | (11.5–22.7) |
| TSH | 0.1 mU/L | (0.35–5.5) |

**Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?**
explanation_md:
Hypophysitis is characterized by inflammation of the pituitary gland and infundibulum leading to hypopituitarism (partial or complete) apart from enlargement of the gland. It can be classified based on the underlying aetiology as primary (e.g. lymphocytic, granulomatous) or secondary (e.g. IgG4-related diseases, immune checkpoint mediators).

| Condition | Example |
|---|---|
| Iatrogenic | CTLA4 inhibitor, PD-1 Ab, interferon α |
| Autoimmune | Polyglandular autoimmune syndrome, post-partum |
| Systemic inflammatory conditions | IgG4-mediated, sarcoidosis, granulomatous with polyangitis |
| Infiltration | Langerhans cell histiocytosis |

Lymphocytic hypophysitis is most commonly reported in women during pregnancy or the post-partum period. It is believed to be an inflammatory/autoimmune disease involving the pituitary gland and its stalk. The presenting symptoms include headache and features of hypopituitarism, such as lethargy, amenorrhoea, polydipsia, and polyuria. In contrast to pituitary adenoma, there is an early involvement of corticotrophs and thyrotrophs. The pituitary gland may be enlarged, leading to optic chiasm compression. MRI may demonstrate a sellar homogeneous mass, together with thickening of the stalk. The definitive diagnosis is established on histology, which shows diffuse lymphocytic infiltration, although biopsy might not be practically feasible in the majority of the patients. Medical management usually involves a conservative approach (pituitary hormone replacement) and the use of steroids.

stem_md:
A 60-year-old man underwent elective trans-sphenoidal surgery for a non-functioning macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm. His post-operative recovery was uneventful. Post-operative day 1 blood test results were as shown:

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 144 mmol/L | (135–145) |
| K | 4.0 mmol/L | (3.5–5.5) |
| Urea | 8.5 mg/dL | (7–20) |
| Creatinine | 110 µmol/L | (60–115) |
| FT4 | 12.0 pmol/L | (11.5–22.7) |
| TSH | 0.8 mU/L | (0.35–5.5) |
| 9 a.m. cortisol | 88 nmol/L | - |

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate step in his management?**
explanation_md:
This patient needs to be started on hydrocortisone replacement therapy, based on low post-operative cortisol levels. His anterior pituitary hormone function should be reassessed 4–6 weeks post-operatively, together with a formal short synacthen test (after withholding the evening dose of hydrocortisone). Repeat MRI of the pituitary should be arranged in 6–8 weeks' time to assess for residual tumour.

| Pituitary function | Screening test | Management |
|---|---|---|
| Central adrenal insufficiency (AI) | Morning cortisol and ACTH; ACTH stimulation test | Hydrocortisone (10–12 mg/m2/day); Steroids may unmask central DI |
| Central hypothyroidism | Serum TSH and FT4 | Exclude central AI before starting thyroxine therapy; Titrate thyroxine dose to aim for FT4 levels in mid to upper half of normal range |
| Central hypogonadism | Gonadotrophins along with 9 a.m. testosterone or oestrogen; Normal menstrual cycles exclude hypogonadism; Exclude hyperprolactinaemia | Testosterone in men (not desiring fertility); Oestrogens (preferably transdermal) in women (not desiring fertility); add progesterone if uterus intact |
| GH deficiency | IGF-1 levels; One or more dynamic tests (insulin tolerance test/GHRH-arginine stimulation test) | GH therapy (subcutaneous): 0.1–1 mg/day in adults; 0.25–0.55 mg/kg/day in children; Exclude AI before replacing GH therapy |

stem_md:
A 70-year-old man underwent elective trans-sphenoidal surgery for a NFPA, which was compressing the optic chiasm. On post-operative day 3, he complained of polydipsia and polyuria. His urine output was noticed to be more than 5 L over a period of 24 hours.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| Na | 148 mmol/L | (135–145) |
| K | 4.6 mmol/L | (3.5–5.5) |
| Urea | 20.5 mg/dL | (7–20) |
| Creatinine | 124 µmol/L | (60–115) |
| Calcium | 2.71 mmol/L | (2.2–2.6) |
| Random glucose | 8.4 mmol/L | - |

**Which one of the following is the most likely aetiology for his symptoms?**
explanation_md: Polydipsia and polyuria during the post-operative period (after trans-sphenoidal surgery) is commonly seen secondary to transient cranial DI. The input/output of patients should be monitored closely. Patients may need desmopressin therapy (intranasally 10–40 µg/day or orally 200–400 µg/day) if symptoms persist, and diagnosis is confirmed based on serum and urine osmolality measurement. There is an increased association of transient DI with intra-operative CSF leak, macroadenoma, craniopharyngioma, and Rathke cleft cyst.

stem_md:
A 55-year-old man complained of an intermittent clear discharge from the nose on a routine follow-up visit to the endocrine clinic. He was a known patient with NFPA who had undergone elective trans-sphenoidal surgery about 6 weeks previously. Post-operatively, he had developed a cerebrospinal fluid leak that required a surgical repair.

**Which one of the following is the most appropriate step in his immediate management?**

options.A: Analyse the nasal discharge for β-transferrin

explanation_md: β transferrin is an isoform of transferrin which is almost exclusively found in CSF. As it is not present in blood, mucus, or tears, it is considered a specific marker of CSF. It is a useful assay in patients where CSF leakage is suspected during the post-operative period.

stem_md:
A 45-year-old man was diagnosed as having acromegaly and underwent elective trans-sphenoidal surgery. Post-operatively, his symptoms of headaches, sweating, and arthralgia persisted. His repeat IGF-1 levels remained elevated, together with unsuppressed growth hormone levels on a glucose tolerance test. As a result, he was started on medical therapy in the form of octreotide long-acting preparation injections, and repeat surgery was planned.

**Which one of the following is a side effect/complication associated with octreotide treatment?**
explanation_md: Octreotide therapy is associated with the development of gallstones and a decrease in gall bladder contractility. Tumour size reduction of >20% is seen in 75% of patients treated with somatostatin analogues. Gastrointestinal side effects, such as anorexia, nausea, vomiting, flatulence, and diarrhoea, commonly develop after the initial injection, with rapid development of tachyphylaxis within 7–14 days. Post-prandial glucose tolerance may be impaired, although gradual adaption develops, and long-term administration of octreotide does not alter glucose homeostasis in normal individuals.

stem_md:
Pasireotide (SOM 230) is a somatostatin analogue, which is approved for treatment of adult patients with surgically incurable Cushing's disease. It has also been shown to be an efficacious agent in the medical management of patients with acromegaly.

**Which one of the following clinical/physiological features is associated with pasireotide (SOM 230) therapy?**

options.A: Increased risk of development of renal stones
options.D: Selective inhibition of somatostatin receptor subtype 2 and 4
options.E: Worsening of glycaemic control in patients with diabetes

explanation_md: Pasireotide (SOM 230) is a somatostatin analogue with a 40-times higher affinity for somatostatin receptor subtype 5 (SST5) as compared to octreotide (which has a relatively higher affinity for SST2). Corticotrophs predominantly express SST5, while GH-producing tumours express SST2 as well as SST5. Pasireotide therapy leads to a decrease in IGF-1 and GH levels, although there is an increased risk of development of gallstones due to the alteration of bile composition and reduced gall bladder wall contractility. SST2 in normal organs adapt (develop tachyphylaxis) to octreotide therapy. In contrast, SST5 in normal organs do not adapt to pasireotide therapy. As a result, its use in patients with Cushing's disease/acromegaly is associated with impairment of glucose metabolism.

stem_md:
A 22-year-old university student presented to the endocrine clinic with a 1-year history of secondary amenorrhoea. She had also experienced symptoms of polydipsia and polyuria for the previous 4 months. Her general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| FSH | 6.0 U/L | (follicular 0.5–5, mid-cycle 8–33, luteal 2–8) |
| LH | 3.3 U/L | (follicular 3–12, mid-cycle 20–80, luteal 3–16) |
| Oestradiol | 22 pmol/L | (follicular 17–260, luteal 180–1100) |
| Prolactin | 775 mU/L | (60–620) |
| FT4 | 10.2 pmol/L | (11.5–22.7 pmol/L) |
| TSH | 0.5 mU/L | (0.35–5.5 mU/L) |
| 9 a.m. cortisol | 352 nmol/L | - |

Water deprivation test:

| Measurement | Result |
|---|---|
| Serum osmolality | 298 mOsmol/Kg |
| Urine osmolality at 6 hours | 202 mOsmol/Kg |
| Urine osmolality after desmopressin acetate (DDAVP) | 780 mOsmol/Kg |

**Which one of the following is the likely diagnosis, based on the water deprivation test results?**

options.E: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)

explanation_md: The water deprivation test involves a serial measurement (2-hourly) of serum and urine osmolality, together with body weight for a period of 6–8 hours in patients suspected to have DI. A serum osmolality of >290 mOsmol/Kg, together with urine osmolality of <300 mOsmol/Kg is suggestive of DI. The diagnosis of central DI is confirmed if there is an increase in urine osmolality >750 mOsmol/Kg after desmopressin. In patients with nephrogenic DI, there is a lack of response to desmopressin. In contrast, patients with psychogenic polydipsia have a low serum osmolality along with appropriate increase in urine osmolality with water deprivation. In clinical practice, the water deprivation test may yield equivocal results due to partial cranial DI or inability to concentrate urine due to a longstanding history of psychogenic polydipsia. Measurement of plasma arginine vasopressin (AVP) or plasma copeptin levels might improve diagnostic accuracy, although these tests have limited availability at this stage.

stem_md:
A 16-year-old boy presented to the endocrine clinic with symptoms of polydipsia and polyuria for the previous 6 months. He was known to have Type 1 DM (diagnosed at age 5 years) and developed severe visual impairment at age 10 years. His initial blood tests showed normal full blood count (FBC), renal function, bone profile, and anterior pituitary function tests. His glycaemic control was good, as reflected by a Glycated Haemoglobin (HbA1c) of 50 mmol/mol.

Water deprivation test (at 6 hours):

| Measurement | Result |
|---|---|
| Serum osmolality | 300 mOsmol/Kg |
| Urine osmolality | 220 mOsmol/Kg |
| Urine osmolality after DDAVP injection | 830 mOsmol/Kg |

**Which one of the following is the likely inheritance pattern of his underlying condition?**
explanation_md: The presence of Type 1 DM, visual impairment (probably secondary to optic atrophy), and DI-based water deprivation test results is consistent with a diagnosis of Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD). This condition has an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. Diabetes and optic atrophy are usually the first manifestations (presenting in the first and second decades), followed by DI (present in 70–80%) and deafness (present in 65–70%) in the second and third decades. The patients may develop features of hypogonadism and progressive neurological disorders, such as ataxia and myoclonus.

stem_md:
An 18-year-old student presented to the endocrine clinic with a 10-month history of secondary amenorrhoea. She also had developed symptoms of polydipsia and polyuria over the previous 4 months. Her general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable. MRI of her pituitary showed a homogenous solid enhancing mass, involving the hypothalamus and pituitary stalk. There was no cystic area and a differential diagnosis of germinoma versus hypophysitis (lymphocytic/granulomatous) was considered.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| FSH | 5.5 U/L | (follicular 0.5–5, mid-cycle 8–33, luteal 2–8) |
| LH | 2.8 U/L | (follicular 3–12, mid-cycle 20–80, luteal 3–16) |
| Oestradiol | 32 pmol/L | (follicular 17–260, luteal 180–1100) |
| Prolactin | 990 mU/L | (60–620) |
| 9 a.m. cortisol | 400 nmol/L | - |
| Fasting blood glucose | 5.5 mmol/L | - |
| Serum calcium | 2.35 mmol/L | (2.2–2.6) |

Water deprivation test:

| Measurement | Result |
|---|---|
| Serum osmolality | 301 mOsmol/Kg |
| Urine osmolality at 6 hours | 205 mOsmol/Kg |
| Urine osmolality after DDAVP | 805 mOsmol/Kg |

**Which one of the following investigations may be helpful to distinguish a germinoma from hypophysitis?**
explanation_md: Germinomas are a rare and heterogeneous group of intracranial tumours. These tumours are most commonly seen in children/young adults and may present with symptoms of anterior pituitary dysfunction and/or DI. The diagnosis of DI in young adults, together with a mass lesion on radiological imaging, should warrant the measurement of serum/CSF β-hCG and α-foetoprotein levels. The definitive diagnosis is based on histological analysis. Immunostaining with markers like NANOG (which is a homeodomain transcription factor) is sensitive, as well as specific for the diagnosis of germinoma, and is considered a better marker than OCT3/4, SOX 2. These tumours are sensitive to radiotherapy, although they may need adjuvant chemotherapy.

options.A: IGF-1 levels and oral glucose tolerance test

explanation_md: The symptoms associated with excess GH/IGF-1 secretion, as seen in acromegaly, includes the coarsening of facial features, an increase in ring/shoe size, prognathism, increased sweating, macroglossia, wide spacing of teeth, and enlargement of extremities. A random serum IGF-1 level measurement is useful for diagnosis (and monitoring of response after therapeutic intervention). Due to variation in GH secretion on a day-to-day basis, a random GH hormone measurement is of limited clinical use. OGTT is a useful test to help establish the underlying diagnosis of acromegaly. It is performed by the consumption of 75 g of oral glucose, followed by half-hourly GH measurement (for 2 hours). A lack of suppression of serum GH <1 ug/L on OGTT (<0.4 ug/L on ultrasensitive assay) is supportive of the diagnosis of acromegaly. In patients with clinical and biochemical evidence of excess GH secretion, MRI of the pituitary should be arranged to identify GH-secreting adenoma.

explanation_md: This case demonstrates co-secretion of GH and prolactin by a pituitary adenoma. Cabergoline therapy can be started immediately to treat hyperprolactinaemia in the outpatient setting and may help shrinkage of the tumour while the patient awaits elective trans-sphenoidal surgery.

stem_md:
A 55-year-old woman was referred to the endocrine clinic with 3–4 weeks' history of feeling generally unwell. She had also been suffering headaches and felt increasingly fatigued. She had a background history of malignant melanoma and had completed a fourth course of ipilimumab therapy 3 months before. On examination, her blood pressure was 90/64 mm of Hg and her pulse was 104/minute with features of dehydration. Visual fields were normal on confrontation testing. MRI of the pituitary showed an enhancing mass with thickening of the pituitary stalk.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| 0-hour cortisol | 72 nmol/L | - |
| 30-minute cortisol (post-synthetic ACTH injection) | 190 nmol/L | - |
| Prolactin | 805 mU/L | (100–550) |
| FT4 | 12.2 pmol/L | (11.5–22.7) |
| TSH | 8.4 mU/L | (0.35–5.5) |

**Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?**
explanation_md: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g. ipilimumab, nivolumab) are being increasingly used in patients with advanced solid tumours such as malignant melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer. Ipilimumab blocks cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4), while nivolumab targets programmed death receptor-1 (PD-1). The use of these agents has been associated with autoimmune hypophysitis (especially ACTH deficiency) and less commonly with thyroiditis.

stem_md:
A 62-year-old man was referred to the endocrine clinic in view of a history of marked fatigue and weight loss. He had a background history of sclerosing cholangitis and salivary gland swelling a few years previously. On examination, he had no palmar or mucosal pigmentation. Visual fields were normal on confrontation. MRI of the pituitary showed an enhancing mass with thickening of the pituitary stalk.

| Investigation | Result | Reference range |
|---|---|---|
| 0-hour cortisol | 116 nmol/L | - |
| 30-minute cortisol (post-synthetic ACTH injection) | 252 nmol/L | - |
| Prolactin | 742 mU/L | (100–550) |
| FT4 | 7.5 pmol/L | (11.5–22.7) |
| TSH | 0.12 mU/L | (0.35–5.5) |

**Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis based on the clinical presentation?**
explanation_md: The background history of sclerosing cholangitis and salivary gland swelling is suggestive of the likely underlying diagnosis of IgG4-related hypophysitis, which is a multisystem disease characterized by infiltration of plasma cells and lymphocytes in one or multiple organs (e.g. skin, retroperitoneum, salivary glands). It can present with features of hypopituitarism (e.g. ACTH and TSH deficiency) along with cranial DI. Although a histopathological confirmation of the diagnosis is considered to be the gold standard, a biopsy is not practically feasible in the majority of the patients. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation, radiological findings (pituitary stalk enlargement), and infiltration of another organ by IgG (or increased IgG levels). The management approach is usually conservative (non-surgical), with steroid therapy (apart from replacement of deficiency pituitary hormones) remaining the mainstay.
